abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: This investigator-initiated, open-label phase 1/2 clinical trial evaluates maveropepimut-S, a survivin-targeting vaccine, combined with pembrolizumab and low-dose cyclophosphamide in patients with recurrent epithelial ovarian cancer (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03029403). The primary endpoints are safety and clinical efficacy measured by overall response rate and disease control rate. Secondary endpoints include recommended phase 2 dose, progression-free survival, overall survival, and survivin-specific immune response. Forty-seven patients are enrolled and forty-four are evaluable. Most treatment-related adverse events are grade 1 or 2, most commonly injection site reactions. The recommended phase 2 dose is 0.25 milliliters. The overall response rate is 23% and the disease control rate is 67%, with greater activity in platinum-sensitive disease. Median progression-free survival is 6.3 months in platinum-sensitive disease and 1.2 months in platinum-resistant disease. Survivin-specific immune responses occur in 62.5% of tested patients and correlate with clinical benefit. The combination demonstrates tolerability and sustained clinical activity.

sec.p: Subject terms: Ovarian cancer, Tumour vaccines

abstract.p: Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) frequently relapses with rising chemoresistance. This phase 1/2 trial evaluates MVP-S vaccination plus pembrolizumab and cyclophosphamide in recurrent EOC, assessing safety, clinical efficacy outcomes, and MVP-S-specific immunity.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Despite significant advances in epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) treatment, it continues to significantly impact women’s health, accounting for an estimated 1.6% of cancer cases and 2.1% of cancer-related deaths in 20221. In the United States, 12,740 women are expected to die annually from ovarian cancer2. Despite important advances in consolidation and maintenance therapy with the addition of bevacizumab and PARP inhibitors3–7, overall survival remains poor due to late detection, high heterogeneity and development of resistance8. Unfortunately, most patients experience multiple relapses until the disease becomes resistant, highlighting a significant unmet need for effective treatments in this setting.

EOC is recognized as a potentially immunogenic tumor, as evidenced by strong correlation between tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and improved outcomes9,10. However, despite transformative success of immunotherapy in other malignancies, these benefits have not translated to EOC. Across numerous phase I–III trials, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), either as monotherapy or combined with chemotherapy or anti-angiogenic therapy, have consistently shown limited clinical activity in recurrent EOC. Response rates remain low, and only one trial assessing pembrolizumab in recurrence in conjunction with weekly paclitaxel/bevacizumab has recently shown significant improvement in progression-free or overall survival11–13. Immunotherapy trials in first-line setting have been similarly disappointing14–16. DUO-O trial enrolled patients without BRCA1/2 mutations in first line and evaluated the addition of durvalumab and olaparib to platinum-based chemotherapy plus bevacizumab. Interim analysis showed improved progression free survival (PFS) in the triplet arm with chemotherapy, bevacizumab and durvalumab followed by maintenance bevacizumab, durvalumab and olaparib compared to control arm (24.2 months versus 19.3 months; HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.52–0.76; P < 0.0001). However, it remains challenging to determine the effect of immunotherapy, as the trial lacked a single durvalumab control arm15. Results from ATHENA-MONO showed that first line maintenance with nivolumab and rucaparib was associated with increased toxicity without PFS benefit16.

Two recent phase III trials have renewed interest in immunotherapy for EOC17,18. FIRST/ENGOT-OV44 explored adding dostarlimab to first-line platinum-based chemotherapy and niraparib maintenance has reported a statistically significant but clinically modest PFS benefit (20.6 vs 19.2 months; HR 0.85), with no overall survival (OS) difference17. In the recurrent platinum-resistant setting, ENGOT-ov65/KEYNOTE-B96 showed that pembrolizumab plus weekly paclitaxel with or without bevacizumab led to PFS gains in the intention to treat (ITT) population (median 8.3 vs 6.4 months; HR 0.73 [95% CI, 0.62–0.86]) and in PD-L1 positive tumors (median 8.3 vs 7.2 months; HR 0.75 [95% CI, 0.61–0.91]). Overall survival results in PD-L1–positive disease are promising but not yet mature (median follow-up 26.6 months): median OS was 18.2 vs 14.0 months (HR 0.76 [95% CI, 0.61–0.94]; P = 0.0053) (ESMO presentation; data not published as yet)18. Therefore, this represents the first phase III trial to suggest a possible OS benefit for an ICI-based regimen in EOC, albeit with incremental gains and in combination with a very active chemotherapy backbone.

Given these limitations, attention has shifted toward next-generation immunotherapy strategies capable of more effectively priming or remodeling the ovarian tumor microenvironment (TME)19. Cancer vaccines are a promising approach in this regard. Survivin, a tumor-associated antigen expressed in 74–90% of ovarian cancers20,21, is a particularly attractive target due to its minimal expression in normal tissue and critical roles in apoptosis inhibition22. Survivin also plays a critical role in mitotic progression during the G2/M phase of cell cycle, further contributing to oncogenesis23. Numerous studies have linked survivin to poor prognostic features and outcomes, such as high grade, advanced stage, p53 mutation, increased resistance to chemotherapy and decreased overall survival21,24,25.

Maveropepimut-S (MVP-S), formerly known as DPX-Survivac, is a novel immunotherapy designed to target and eliminate survivin-expressing tumor cells through the action of educated cytotoxic T cells. The DPX technology is a non-aqueous, lipid-in-oil, immune-educating delivery platform. MVP-S is formulated with five HLA-restricted class I peptides derived from survivin, a T helper peptide (A16L), and the innate immune stimulant poly dIdC. When injected subcutaneously, the oil-based delivery system forms a depot at the injection site. This formulation promotes active and sustained uptake of the target peptides by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) at the injection site, which then prime a de novo survivin-specific CD8+ T cell response capable of infiltrating tumor tissues. Preclinically, this combination resulted in expanded clonality with consequently less diverse T-cell population promoting effective immune responses within the TME26.

A previous phase I study demonstrated that immune modulation with cyclophosphamide enhanced the immunogenicity of MVP-S in ovarian cancer by inhibiting suppressive immune cells such as Tregs27. Following this observation, our team initiated a phase I/Ib study to evaluate MVP-S at different dose levels, both alone and combined with cyclophosphamide, in patients with EOC who had no evidence of disease progression post chemotherapy. This study confirmed the safety of the combination and showed increased immune responses with the addition of cyclophosphamide28. Overall, considering the available data, the combination of MVP-S with cyclophosphamide showed immune responses and durable clinical benefit28–30.

To date, clinical experience with MVP-S in EOC has shown a tolerable safety profile, primarily consisting of injection site reactions (ISRs) and fatigue29,31,32. Immunologically, the addition of ICI, such as anti-PD-1, has the potential to expand antigen-specific T-cells and inhibit regulatory T-cells (Tregs), thereby enhancing the overall tumor immune response26,33. Preclinical data suggest a synergistic effect between ICIs and cancer vaccines, particular through activation of tumor reactive CD8+ TILs34. Consequently, Conter and colleagues carried out a basket trial combining pembrolizumab with MVP-S and cyclophosphamide in patients with advanced solid tumors, including 8 patients with ovarian cancer35. Concurrently, other studies were initiated adding pembrolizumab to MVP-S and cyclophosphamide in metastatic bladder cancer36 and recurrent/refractory diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL)33. Across these studies, this combination was well-tolerated and demonstrated encouraging clinical responses.

Together, these findings let to the design of the PESCO trial (NCT03029403), the first phase 1/2 study evaluating the combination MVP-S, pembrolizumab and intermittent low-dose cyclophosphamide in patient with advanced ovarian cancer (Fig. 1). The study was designed to assess the safety immunogenicity, and preliminary clinical activity of this regimen across distinct setting including platinum-sensitive and platinum resistant-disease as well as less common histologic subtypes. In addition to clinical outcomes, the trial incorporated longitudinal collection of blood and tumor biopsies for correlative analysis. Here, we report the clinical outcomes, survivin-specific immune responses and HLA genotyping analyses.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between February 2018 and May 2023, 56 patients were consented and screened for eligibility. Seven patients screen failed, and 2 patients declined. In total, 47 patients were enrolled, 16 in dose escalation and 31 patients in the dose expansion cohorts. However, 3 patients experienced disease progression before receiving the first dose and subsequently withdrew from the study. Therefore, 44 patients were evaluable for safety and efficacy analyses (Fig. 2). Data were collected until March 2024. Patient demographics and baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The median age was 60 (range, 38–78) years. The median prior lines of systemic therapies were 2 (range 1–7). In the dose escalation, 10 patients had high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), 2 patients had clear cell carcinoma (CCC), and 2 patients had mixed histologies, including endometrioid and sarcoma, and HGSC and carcinosarcoma. Expansion cohorts A and B were composed of patients with ovarian HGSC. Exploratory cohort C of less common histologies included 2 patients with low-grade serous carcinoma, and 8 patients with CCC. The median cycles of treatment in all patients were 4 (range, 1–34) and median doses of MVP-S were 2 (range 1–8).

sec.p: In the dose escalation, 14 patients were evaluable for safety, 8 patients received dose level 1 (0.25 mL) and 6 patients received dose level 2 (0.5 mL). In the dose expansion, 10 patients were evaluable in each cohort (platinum-sensitive, platinum resistant and exploratory). As of March 2024, the median study follow-up was 14 (range, 1.3–39.1) months.

sec.title: Dose escalation and RP2D
sec.p: DLTs were assessed during the first cycle of treatment (first 21 days). Initially, three patients were treated at dose level 1, with one patient experiencing grade 3 nephritis and proteinuria. Following this, the safety committee recommended enrolling three additional patients at dose level 1. Among them, one patient did not complete the first cycle due to disease progression. This patient was replaced. No further DLTs were observed, allowing the study to proceed to dose level 2 after 7 patients enrolled.

At dose level 2, three patients were included, with one patient experiencing grade 3 nephritis. Consequently, additional three patients were enrolled at dose level 2 (n = 6). One of these patients developed grade 3 ISR. After reviewing the data, the safety committee recommended de-escalating the dose and enrolling two additional patients at dose level 1 to confirm safety and determine RP2D (a total of 8 patients at dose level 1). No other DLTs were observed, and dose level 1 was declared the RP2D. Expansion cohorts A, B and C were subsequently opened.

sec.title: Clinical efficacy
sec.p: The best responses according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1 criteria for the dose escalation and expansion cohorts A and B are summarized in Table 2. Among 14 patients evaluable for efficacy in dose escalation, 1 had complete response (CR), 2 had partial response (PR), and 6 had stable disease (SD), resulting in an overall response rate (ORR) of 21.4% (95% CI: 7.6–47.6%) and a disease control rate (DCR) of 64.3% (95% CI: 38.8–83.7%).

sec.p: In the platinum sensitive cohort A, 4 of 10 patients (40.0%; 95% CI: 16.8–68.7%) achieved PR, and 5 patients (50%) had SD, leading to a DCR of 90.0% (95% CI: 59.6–98.2%). In the platinum resistant cohort B, 1 of 10 patients (10.0%; 95% CI: 1.8–40.4%) had PR, and 3 patients (30%) had SD, with 2 patients maintaining SD for more than 12 weeks. This resulted in a DCR of 40.0% (95% CI: 16.8–68.7%). The predefined signal of activity for the expansion cohorts was met.

Across dose escalation and expansion cohorts A and B, the ORR was 23% (95% CI: 12.4–40.0%), and the DCR was 67% (95% CI: 50.8–80.9%). Twenty-nine (61%) patients enrolled had high grade serous carcinoma. In this subgroup, the ORR was 24% (95% CI: 12.2–42.1%), with a DCR of 82% (95% CI: 65.5–92.4%), with 7 patients achieving PR and 17 achieving SD. (Fig. 3). There was a significant difference in median PFS between cohort A (platinum sensitive) and B (platinum resistant). The median PFS was 6.3 (95% CI: 0.9–10.8) months in cohort A, and 1.2 (95% CI: 1.0–4.1) months in cohort B (P = 0.016) (Fig. 4A). Median OS was not reached in cohort A, while in cohort B, the median OS was 10.7 months (95% CI: 3.5-not reached) (P = 0.15) (Fig. 4B).

sec.p: In exploratory cohort C, the ORR was 20% (95% CI: 5.7–51.0%), and DCR was 40% (95% CI: 16.8–68.7%), with 2 of 10 patients achieving PR and 2 achieving SD. Among the 8 patients with CCC in cohort C, one had PR and one had SD. Across dose escalation and cohort C, 10 patients had CCC and 1 had mixed CCC and endometrioid histology; among them, 1 had CR, 2 had PR, and 2 SD, yielding an ORR of 27.3% (95% CI: 9.7–56.6%) and a DCR of 45.5% (95% CI: 21.3–72.0%). The best percentage change in target lesions and longitudinal tumor burden changes during treatment for patients in expansion cohorts A, B and C are presented in Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2, respectively. Across all 44 patients, the ORR was 22.7% (95% CI: 12.8–37.0%), and DCR was 61.4% (95% CI: 46.6–74.3%). Kaplan–Meier estimates of PFS and OS for all patients are reported in Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4, respectively.

A patient on dose escalation (PESCO-016) with mismatch repair (MMR) deficient mixed endometrioid and CCC, completed 34 cycles of treatment, 2 of them with MVP-S which was discontinued due to ISR. She had CR after 8 cycles which is ongoing 30 months after her last dose of treatment discontinued due to maximum benefit. Flow cytometry analysis of memory T cell and survivin response is available in Supplementary Fig. 5. In cohort A, one patient (PESCO-030) received only 1 cycle of treatment and discontinued due to aseptic meningitis. Despite early discontinuation, she maintained PR for 31 months without any oncological treatment. Another patient in cohort A (PESCO-038), completed 17 cycles of treatment including 8 MVP-S doses and discontinued due to grade 3 ISR. This patient maintained a sustained PR for 22 months following treatment discontinuation. The association between ISRs and clinical response was assessed. Specifically, the relationship between both any-grade ISR and grade 3 ISR with objective response (responder vs. non-responder) was analyzed. In both analyses, no significant association was observed between ISR occurrence and clinical response.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Among the 44 (93.6%) patients who received at least one dose of treatment, all were included in the safety analysis. The median doses of MVP-S administered was 2 (range 1–8). Figure 5 summarizes the most frequent Treatment related adverse events (TRAEs). ISR were the most common TRAE, occurring in 33 of 44 (75%) patients. They were usually grade 1–2 presenting with symptoms such as erythema, induration, pain, warmth, and hyperpigmentation. Grade 3 ISR occurred in 6 (13.6%) patients, all presenting with ulceration and led to discontinuation of MVP-S in each case. Other frequent TRAEs were fatigue (45.4%), anemia (43.2%), nausea (36.3%), pruritus (27.2%), skin rash (20.4%), and diarrhea (20.4%). We also explored whether the occurrence of ISR was associated with clinical response. In exploratory analyses, neither the presence of grade 3 ISR nor ISR of any grade showed a statistically significant association with response status.

sec.p: One patient presented with grade 4 creatine phosphokinase (CPK) elevation associated with grade 3 hypothyroidism. Work-up was negative for myositis, and CPK levels normalized with hydration and thyroid replacement therapy.

One patient had grade 3 aseptic meningitis after 1 cycle. This patient was admitted with headache, fever, and nausea. On investigation, brain MRI was normal but lumbar puncture showed elevated white blood cells with 99% of lymphocytes, all cultures were negative. Patient had clinical improvement with oral steroids. This was considered TRAE related to the combination and treatment was discontinued.

Two cases of immune-related nephritis were reported and were considered related to the treatment combination at the time of investigator assessment. At dose level 1, one patient (PESCO-003) developed grade 3 proteinuria after two cycles of treatment. Renal biopsy confirmed immune-mediated membranous nephropathy. The patient was treated with corticosteroids and discontinued from the trial. Upon subsequent rechallenge with pembrolizumab off-study, proteinuria recurred after a single cycle. At dose level 2, another patient (PESCO-010) developed grade 3 increase in serum creatinine following three cycles. Renal biopsy findings were consistent with immune-mediated interstitial nephritis. The patient responded to corticosteroid therapy with resolution of renal dysfunction and was withdrawn from the study.

sec.title: Survivin-specific immune responses
sec.p: Survivin-specific CD8+ T-cell responses induced by MVP-S were measured by interferon-gamma (IFNγ) production following MHC class I-restricted peptide pool re-stimulation using peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) samples collected at multiple time points during the treatment (Fig. 6). Among 24 patients tested, control TT vaccine epitope-specific responses were rapidly induced in 22 (92%) patients, regardless of clinical response, confirming intact immune competence (Figs. 6A, B). Memory CMV-, EBV-, and Flu-specific responses did not significantly differ between clinical responders (CR, PR) and non-responders (SD, PD). Fifteen patients (62.5%) had survivin-specific responses, defined as IFNγ detection in greater than 0.1% of CD8+ T cells (Figs. 6C, D). Survivin-specific immune responses were enriched in patients with clinical benefit: 1/1 (100%) with CR, 7/7 (100%) with PR, 6/9 (66.7%) with SD demonstrated response, whereas only 2/7 (28.6%) of PD patients showed a response (Fig. 6D). Importantly, persistence of these responses beyond early treatment cycles was observed almost exclusively in patients who experienced clinical benefit. Overall, 14 of 15 survivin-specific responders (93.3%) derived clinical benefit. In cohort A, a patient with HGSC (PESCO-042) exhibited the strongest immune response detected 21 weeks after the first dose of MVP-S, which correlated with radiological PR (Supplementary Fig. 5). She received 12 cycles of treatment and 6 doses of MVP-S, until she developed grade 3 ISR. Treatment was paused for 5 months until she had PD. PESCO-016, discussed above, had the longest survivin-specific immune response, lasting 195 weeks from cycle 1 (Supplementary Fig. 5).

sec.p: Patients were not pre-screened for HLA compatibility, as MVP-S incorporates peptides restricted by five HLA class I molecules (A1, A2, A3, A24, B7) that are broadly represented across the human population (Supplementary Table 1). HLA typing was performed in the exploratory analysis to investigate potential associations with vaccine-induced IFNγ responses. Alleles directly linked to the MVP-S epitopes (A01, A02, A03, A24, B07) were variably distributed across clinical response groups. HLA-A*24:02 was detected in CR, PR, and SD but absent in PD (Supplementary Fig. 6), raising the possibility that presence of the A24 allele may confer a propensity for clinical benefit in response to survivin peptide vaccination. A01 and A02 were identified in PR, SD, and PD patients, A03 in SD and PD, and B07 only in SD, indicating no clear enrichment in responders. Structural superfamily overlap was also observed, as in PESCO-029, a PR patient with strong IFNγ responses who had no vaccine-restricted alleles but was homozygous for A11:01, an A3 superfamily allele reported to bind Survivin epitopes. Conversely, several PD patients carried two vaccine-restricted alleles but failed to mount IFNγ responses, indicating that presence of relevant HLA alleles alone did not predict immunogenicity.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this phase 1/2 trial, we evaluated the novel combination of MVP-S, pembrolizumab, and intermittent low-dose cyclophosphamide in patients with advanced EOC. In dose escalation, RP2D of MVP-S was established at 0.25 mL (dose level 1) after initial priming. The combination met the primary endpoints with an ORR of 24%, and a DCR of 82% in patients with HGSC or endometrioid histologies. Clinical benefit was more pronounced in patients with platinum-sensitive disease, who achieved an ORR of 40% and a DCR of 90%. However, encouraging signals were also observed in patients with platinum-resistant disease, where outcomes exceeded expectations with an ORR of 16% and a DCR of 54%, compared to the standard-of-care single-agent chemotherapy, which typically achieves an ORR around 11.8%37. These findings suggest that this combination may provide disease control in a population with limited treatment options.

Our results build on prior studies of MVP-S, including the DECIDE trial, in which MVP-S and cyclophosphamide was evaluated in 22 patients with advanced EOC and demonstrated an ORR of 21% and a DCR of 63%29. The addition of pembrolizumab in our study appears to enhance immunogenicity, underscoring its potential role in boosting survivin-specific T-cell responses. Similar to the DECIDE trial, our study observed survivin-specific T-cell responses in most patients tested, with some showing durable effects. Stronger IFNγ responses were associated with improved disease control, aligning with preclinical evidence supporting the synergy between ICI and therapeutic vaccination. Overall, prior peptide vaccine studies in ovarian cancer establish immunogenicity with limited standalone efficacy, reinforcing the biological rationale for combination strategies to overcome the immunosuppressive environment and translate immune activation into clinical benefit38.

Although the vaccine covers a wide range of HLA types, variability in immune responses may reflect differences in antigen presentation. HLA typing revealed that while A2402 was consistently present in CR, PR, and SD but absent in PD, other vaccine-restricted alleles (A01, A02, A03, B07) were also found among non-responders, and some patients with strong IFNγ responses lacked these alleles but carried cross-presenting variants such as A11. This complexity suggests that allele-specific and superfamily-level interactions, together with reduced HLA class I heterozygosity observed more frequently in SD and PD, may influence both immunogenicity and clinical outcomes. These results underscore the plausibility that HLA genotype contributes to the variability of vaccine-induced immunity, but also highlight the need for more comprehensive bioinformatic analyses in larger cohorts to clarify the clinical relevance of these associations.

The safety profile of the combination was manageable and consistent with prior MVP-S studies29,31,39. Local ISRs were the most common TRAEs (75%), predominantly grade 1–2, with grade 3 events in 13.6% of patients. This incidence is lower than the 22.7% reported in the DECIDE trial, which did not include a checkpoint inhibitor. Two cases of immune-related nephritis and one case of aseptic meningitis were observed, all of which improved following corticosteroid therapy. These TRAEs were considered related to the combination of MVP-S and pembrolizumab. However, pembrolizumab has been associated with both nephritis and aseptic meningitis, although these are rare occurrences40–43. In one patient with biopsy-confirmed membranous nephropathy experienced recurrence of proteinuria upon rechallenge with pembrolizumab off-study, suggesting a potential contribution from antiPD-1 therapy. It is challenging to determine the relative contribution of each individual immunotherapy agent to the observed toxicities, but overall, the safety profile does not suggest an increase in systemic or local toxicities with the addition of pembrolizumab to MVP-S and low-dose cyclophosphamide. When compared to previous MVP-S studies, including the DECIDE trial, the incidence of systemic adverse events in our cohort was comparable and within the expected range27–29,32,33. These findings suggest that the addition of pembrolizumab did not exacerbate local vaccine-related toxicity.

Case series, reports, clinical trials and subgroup analyses from ovarian cancer immunotherapy trials suggest that CCC histology may derive greater benefit from immunotherapy13,44–46. This is supported by microenvironment analyses of ovarian CCC, which highlight predictive biomarkers for immune response, particularly in the context of ARID1A mutations47. Despite the small sample size of 11 patients with ovarian CCC in PESCO trial, five demonstrated clinical benefit, including one patient with an MMR-deficient tumor who achieved a sustained CR. These findings underscore the importance of assessing MMR status in EOC and reinforce the evidence for the potential role of immunotherapy in CCC. Further investigation of immunotherapy combinations is warranted in this population.

In this study, 62.5% of patients tested experienced vaccine-specific T-cell responses and 86.7% of these patients had disease control (CR, PR or SD). These findings suggest that the combination MVP-S/pembrolizumab/cyclophosphamide has the potential to bypass local immune tolerance in the TME and induce T-cell responses in ovarian cancer. As we measured the immune response in aggregate against the survivin peptide fragment pool, it was not possible to assess whether responses differ by survivin peptide. Future investigations could examine immune responses to a single epitope. Manning-Geist et al. recently published a Phase I trial combining WT1 peptide vaccine (Galinpepimut-S) with anti-PD-1, nivolumab, in patients with advanced ovarian cancer. Among 11 patients enrolled, 91% developed WT1-specific T cell responses and produced IgG antibodies48. Additionally, the 1-year PFS rate was 70%, which was linked to the presence of WT1-specific immune responses. These results were similar to our findings of durable clinical responses and long-lasting antigen-specific immune responses.

PESCO trial had a number of limitations. As a single arm, non-randomized trial, the absence of a control arm precludes the ability to draw definitive conclusions regarding clinical efficacy, and the small sample size limits the statistical power. Cohort C included uncommon histologies and was exploratory by design, without power for inferential analyses. Correlative immune data were hypothesis-generating and not adjusted for multiple comparisons. In addition, immune monitoring was performed using pooled survivin epitopes, precluding assessment of responses at the level of individual peptides. Despite these constraints, our data demonstrate clinically meaningful activity and long-lasting survivin-specific T-cell responses in a population with limited treatment options.

Nevertheless, this study highlights survivin as a potential novel target in ovarian cancer, demonstrating significant clinical responses. Given the small sample size is not possible to determine the impact of BRCA mutation or even prior therapies such as bevacizumab and poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors in the outcomes. Survivin-specific immune responses were associated with disease control, and exploratory HLA analyses highlight the importance of antigen presentation in shaping clinical outcomes. Refining patient selection based on HLA matching or survivin expression could further enhance the therapeutic benefit of the MVP-S/pembrolizumab/cyclophosphamide combination.

As part of our correlative studies, ongoing analyses of immune microenvironment and survivin expression will also be crucial in identifying potential biomarkers predictive of response. More recently, biomarker driven therapies are becoming part of clinical practice, such as Mirvetuximab soravtansine for ovarian cancer with high expression of folate receptor alpha49. Thus, the identification of novel targets and the enrichment of patient selection based on specific biomarkers hold the potential to expand therapeutic options in ovarian cancer.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: PESCO is an investigator-initiated, open-label, non-randomized, single-center phase 1/2 trial evaluating the combination of MVP-S, pembrolizumab, and intermittent low-dose cyclophosphamide in patients with EOC. The trial complied with all relevant ethical regulators. The protocol was approved by the Ontario Cancer Research Ethics Board (OCREB) and Health Canada. The trial was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03029403) on 20 January 2017, prior to patient enrollment. All patients provided written informed consent. Patient confidentiality and data privacy were maintained throughout the clinical trial. The study design and conduct complied with all relevant regulations regarding the use of human study participants and was conducted in accordance with the criteria set by the Declaration of Helsinki, International Council for Harmonisation Good Clinical Practice guidelines as well as Health Canada Division 5 regulations. There was no compensation for study participants.

A standard 3 + 3 dose-escalation design was employed to determine the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) as demonstrated in Fig. 1. The primary objective of the escalation phase was to determine the toxicity profile and establish the RP2D for further evaluation in expansion cohorts. During the dose escalation, two dose levels of MVP-S were evaluated in patients with platinum-resistant EOC: dose level 1 (0.25 mL) and dose level 2 (0.5 mL), both administered every 6 weeks (every other cycle) after an initial priming dose. MVP-S was administered subcutaneously to alternating upper thighs. Pembrolizumab 200 mg was administered intravenously every 3 weeks, and oral cyclophosphamide 50 mg BID was given starting 7 days before MVP-S dosing, continuing a 7-day on, 7-day off schedule. Treatment continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or consent withdraw.

Following the dose escalation, dose expansion cohorts were initiated. In this phase, patients with high-grade serous or endometrioid carcinoma were treated at the RP2D in three cohorts: cohort A, consisting of patients with platinum-sensitive disease, defined as those whose disease recurred more than 6 months after the last platinum-based chemotherapy; cohort B, comprising patients with platinum-resistant disease, defined as those whose disease recurred within 6 months of the last platinum-based chemotherapy; and exploratory cohort C, which included patients with uncommon histologies such as clear cell, mucinous, and low-grade serous or endometrioid ovarian carcinomas.

Adverse events were monitored throughout the trial and graded in severity according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 4.03. ISRs were clinically evaluated, measured and photographed at each clinic visit. Dose limiting toxicities (DLTs) were assessed during the first cycle of treatment in the dose escalation phase. DLTs included all grade 4 non hematologic toxicity or grade 3 lasting for more than 3 days; grade 3 laboratory value that persisted for more than 1 week or required medical intervention; grade 3 or 4 febrile neutropenia; grade 2 or greater allergic reaction, urticaria or autoimmune reactions (except for vitiligo or fever for less than 2 days); ISR with grade 2 or greater ulceration persisting for more than a week.

sec.title: Patient selection
sec.p: Women aged 18 years or older with advanced epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer were eligible for enrollment. In the dose-escalation, all histological subtypes with platinum resistant disease were permitted. For the subsequent dose-expansion cohorts, patients with high-grade serous or endometrioid ovarian carcinoma were enrolled into cohort A if they had platinum-sensitive disease, or cohort B if they had platinum-resistant disease. Patients with non-high grade serous ovarian carcinoma were included in the exploratory cohort C regardless of platinum sensitivity. Eligibility criteria included measurable disease according to RECIST 1.1 criteria, a life expectancy of more than 16 weeks, and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1. Prior exposure to immunotherapy, including anti-PD-1, anti-PDL1, or anti-PDL2 agents, was not permitted. In the dose-escalation phase and exploratory cohort C, patients could have received any number of prior treatment lines. However, in expansion cohorts A and B, no more than four prior lines of therapy were permitted.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: Subjects were evaluated at baseline and every 6 weeks (42 days ±7 days) with radiographic imaging to assess response to treatment by RECIST 1.1 criteria. Patients had mandatory image-guided fresh tumor core biopsy at baseline and day 15 of cycle 1. A biopsy at the time of radiological progression was optional. Opportunistic biopsy or cytology sample from fluid collection was used for exploratory analysis. Peripheral blood and serum were obtained at baseline and at several time points during investigational treatment (Fig. 1).

After the end of treatment, each subject was followed for 30 days for adverse event monitoring. Serious adverse events (SAEs) were collected for 90 days after the end of treatment. Subjects who discontinued treatment for reasons other than disease progression had post-treatment follow-up of disease status until disease progression, initiating a non-study cancer treatment, withdrawing consent, or becoming lost to follow-up. All subjects were followed for overall survival until death, withdrawal of consent or the end of the study, whichever comes first, for a maximum of 2 years.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary objective was to evaluate the safety of the combination and establish the RP2D of MVP-S. Clinical anti-tumor activity of the combination of pembrolizumab, MVP-S and oral cyclophosphamide was also a primary endpoint. Dose escalation and dose expansion cohorts A and B were included in the efficacy endpoint analysis. The exploratory cohort C was analyzed separately. Efficacy was evaluated based on DCR and ORR, according to RECIST 1.1 criteria. Secondary objectives included PFS, OS, and efficacy in both platinum sensitive and platinum resistant disease, and in less common ovarian cancer subtypes.

The translational objectives included investigating the immunogenicity of MVP-S by assessing survivin-specific immune responses in patients who received more than two treatment cycles or had an end-of-treatment (EOT) or follow-up blood sample collected more than 30 days after vaccination. HLA-typing was performed in all patients.

sec.title: Survivin-specific immune response assay
sec.p: Fresh whole blood samples (5 ml) were diluted to 20 ml with PBS followed by centrifugation at 400 × g for 5 min and removal of the supernatant. Red blood cells were lysed with 5 ml AcK solution (Lonza) for 10 min at room temperature followed by centrifugation at 400 × g for 5 min and removal of the supernatant. PBMC pellets were resuspended in complete RPMI plus 10% DMSO at 1 × 106 cells per ml, slow-frozen and stored in liquid nitrogen (vapor phase) until use. PBMCs were plated at 2.5 × 105 cells per well in a 96 well U-bottom plate in a total of 200 μl of RPMI media containing 5% human AB serum, Penicillin/Streptomycin, and beta-mercapto-ethanol. Expansion of antigen-specific T cells was achieved by the addition of 10 ng/ml IL-2 and IL-15 and either 1 μM each of the 5 Survivin peptides contained in MVP-S or the helper peptide (TT A16L), or a 23 peptide “CEF” pool derived from hCMV, EBV and Influenza{Currier, 2002, PMID: 11792386}. Half the media was removed every 3–4 days, and an equal volume of fresh media containing IL-2 and IL-15 added back, and the cells split 1:2, with addition of fresh media and cytokines, as needed. After 14–18 days, expanded cells were harvested, washed, and replated in fresh media containing 1 μg/ml brefeldin A and each test peptide pool, and incubated at 37 C in a humidified incubator for 4.5 h. Re-stimulated cells were then washed and stained with anti-CD8-PerCP and fixable viability dye, followed by fixation in 2% PFA, permeabilization in 0.02% saponin, intracellular staining with anti-IFNγ-APC, wash, and final fixation in 2% PFA. Production of IFNγ in CD8+ T cells was measured by flow cytometry, and quantitated as % CD8+IFNγ+ cells of total cells using FlowJo for Mac (Version 10.9). Background IFNγ+ cell frequencies observed in baseline screening blood samples were generally less than 0.05%, and greater than twice background (0.1%) IFNγ+CD8+ cell frequencies were considered positive for vaccine induced T cell responses.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The dose escalation followed a standard 3 + 3 design. A dose level was considered safe if no more than one DLT occurred among six treated patients. TRAEs were summarized by frequency and severity according to NCI CTCA version 4.03. The treatment efficacy was defined based on ORR as per RECIST v1.1 criteria. A predefined signal of activity to justify opening dose expansion cohorts required at least 3 out of 10 PR or SD lasting ≥12 weeks in the platinum-sensitive cohort and 2 out of 10 for the platinum-resistant cohort.

Participant demographics, baseline characteristics, safety and efficacy outcomes are summarized using descriptive statistics. Efficacy endpoints were analyzed in the evaluable patients. PFS and OS were estimated using Kaplan–Meier method, and comparisons between cohorts were performed using the log-rank test. Binomial 95% confidence intervals for ORR and DCR were calculated using the Wilson score method. A general linear mixed model was used to explore IFNγ responses and their association with clinical outcomes. Exploratory analyses were conducted to assess preliminary response signals in the less common subtypes.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The raw subject-level clinical data generated and analyzed during this study contain potentially identifiable patient information and are protected under data privacy legislation and institutional Research Ethics Board requirements. These data are therefore not publicly available. De-identified individual participant data underlying the summary statistics and figures reported in this Article are provided as a Source Data file with this paper. Additional de-identified data may be made available to qualified academic investigators for non-commercial research purposes upon reasonable request, subject to approval by the University Health Network Research Ethics Board and execution of a data-sharing agreement. Requests should be directed to the corresponding author (A.M.O.; amit.oza@uhn.ca). Data access requests will be reviewed within approximately 60 days of receipt of a complete proposal. Approved data will be made available for a defined period under the terms of the data-sharing agreement. The study protocol is available in Supplementary Note 2 within the Supplementary Information. All other data supporting the findings of this study are available within the Article and its Supplementary Information. Source data are provided with this paper.
